q1.prompt: In Snowflake's RBAC model, privileges are granted to:

a.text: Roles — then roles are assigned to users
a.feedback: Correct! The chain is privilege → role → user. You grant to roles, not directly to users.

b.text: Users directly — roles are just labels
b.feedback: Not quite — Snowflake uses Role-Based Access Control. Privileges go to roles, and roles are granted to users.

c.text: Databases — then users inherit from the database
c.feedback: Databases don't hold privileges on behalf of users. Privileges are granted to roles.

d.text: Schemas — which pass them down to tables automatically
d.feedback: Schemas don't distribute privileges. Each level (database, schema, table) requires its own explicit grant to the role.

q2.prompt: To successfully query a table, your role needs grants at which levels?

a.feedback: Correct! All four links in the chain are required. Missing any one = access denied.

b.text: Just SELECT on the table — the rest is automatic
b.feedback: No — Snowflake requires grants at every level. Without USAGE on the database or schema, you can't even see the table.

c.feedback: Close, but you also need USAGE on the warehouse (for compute) and USAGE on the schema (to see objects inside it).

d.text: ACCOUNTADMIN role — only admins can query tables
d.feedback: Any role can query a table as long as it has the full grant chain. ACCOUNTADMIN is not required for reading data.

q3.prompt: You see the error: "Object 'FEEDBACK' does not exist or not authorized." What does this most likely mean?

a.text: Your current role doesn't have a grant to access that table — the table still exists
a.feedback: Correct! Snowflake uses this vague message deliberately to avoid revealing what objects exist to unauthorized roles. The fix is a GRANT, not a CREATE.

b.text: The table was dropped and no longer exists
b.feedback: While possible, this message almost always means a missing privilege — not a missing table. Check your grants first.

c.text: The table is corrupted and needs to be recreated
c.feedback: Snowflake tables don't "corrupt" this way. The error means your role lacks a privilege on the object.

d.text: You need to run USE DATABASE first to refresh the cache
d.feedback: USE DATABASE sets context but won't help if the role lacks grants. The fix is granting the missing privilege.

q4.prompt: What does USE SECONDARY ROLES ALL do?

a.text: Combines privileges from all your granted roles with your primary role — expanding effective access
a.feedback: Correct! Secondary roles let you access data from all your granted roles without switching. Your primary role still controls object ownership.

b.text: Switches your primary role to a different role
b.feedback: That would be USE ROLE. Secondary roles keep your primary role unchanged and add other roles' privileges on top.

c.text: Grants new privileges permanently to your primary role
c.feedback: Secondary roles don't create new grants — they activate existing roles you already have for the current session only.

d.feedback: It only activates roles already granted to you. If you don't have ACCOUNTADMIN, you won't get its privileges.

q1.prompt: What do GRANT SELECT ON FUTURE TABLES IN SCHEMA statements do?

a.text: Automatically grant SELECT on every table created in that schema from now on
a.feedback: Correct! Future grants apply to objects that don't exist yet. Any new table created in the schema will automatically get the specified grant.

b.text: Grant SELECT on all tables that currently exist in the schema
b.feedback: That's what ON ALL TABLES does. ON FUTURE TABLES only covers tables created after the statement runs — you need both for complete coverage.

c.text: Grant SELECT on tables in all schemas across the database
c.feedback: Future grants are scoped to the specific schema (or database) named in the statement, not all schemas.

d.text: Temporarily grant SELECT until the table is dropped
d.feedback: Future grants are permanent (until explicitly revoked). They're not time-limited or tied to table lifecycle.

q2.prompt: Why should a data engineer include GRANT statements in the same script as CREATE TABLE?

a.text: Because a table nobody can read is effectively invisible — grants are part of deployment, not an afterthought
a.feedback: Correct! CREATE + GRANT ship together as one atomic unit. If you separate them, there's a window where consumers can't access the data — and manual grant requests create bottlenecks.

b.text: Because Snowflake requires it — CREATE TABLE fails without a GRANT in the same transaction
b.feedback: Snowflake doesn't require them together. It's a best practice, not a technical requirement. Tables can exist without any grants.

c.text: Because GRANT statements must come before CREATE TABLE in Snowflake
c.feedback: Actually GRANT comes after CREATE — you can't grant on an object that doesn't exist yet. The best practice is to include them together in the same script.

d.text: Because tables are automatically dropped if not granted within 24 hours
d.feedback: There's no auto-drop. Tables persist indefinitely without grants — they just can't be seen by other roles. The reason to co-deploy is operational, not technical.

q3.prompt: You've set up ON FUTURE TABLES grants but existing tables are still inaccessible. What's missing?

a.text: You also need GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES — future grants don't cover tables that already exist
a.feedback: Correct! ON FUTURE only covers objects created after the grant. You need ON ALL TABLES for existing objects. Always pair both for complete coverage.

b.text: You need to drop and recreate the existing tables for future grants to apply
b.feedback: That's destructive and unnecessary. Just run GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES to cover existing objects alongside your future grants.

c.text: Future grants take 24 hours to propagate to existing objects
c.feedback: Future grants never propagate to existing objects — that's by design. Use ON ALL TABLES for objects that already exist.

d.text: You need to run ALTER TABLE ... REFRESH GRANTS on each table
d.feedback: There's no such command. The solution is to run GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES alongside ON FUTURE TABLES.

q4.prompt: What is the recommended schema design pattern to simplify access management?

a.text: Separate data by sensitivity level into different schemas — use schema-wide grants for analytics, per-object grants for sensitive data
a.feedback: Correct! Schema-as-access-boundary: analytics data gets schema-wide future grants, sensitive/PII data lives in a restricted schema with per-object grants. This eliminates most manual grant work.

b.text: Put all tables in one schema and use per-object grants for everything
b.feedback: This works but doesn't scale. With hundreds of tables, per-object grants become an operational nightmare. Separating by sensitivity lets you use schema-wide grants for most data.

c.text: Give all roles ACCOUNTADMIN access to avoid grant issues entirely
c.feedback: This violates least privilege and is a major security risk. ACCOUNTADMIN should never be used for day-to-day work or granted broadly.

d.text: Create a separate database for each user to avoid sharing entirely
d.feedback: This defeats the purpose of a shared data platform. The goal is controlled sharing — schemas by sensitivity level with appropriate grants at each level.

q1.prompt: What is the key difference between a Managed Access schema and a normal schema?

a.text: In a Managed Access schema, only the schema owner can grant access — even on tables created by others
a.feedback: Correct! This centralizes grant control. Engineers can still create objects, but they can't share them without the admin's approval — preventing accidental exposure of sensitive data.

b.text: In a Managed Access schema, nobody can create tables except the schema owner
b.feedback: Not quite — anyone with CREATE TABLE privilege can still create tables. The restriction is on granting, not creating.

c.text: Managed Access schemas automatically encrypt all data at rest
c.feedback: All Snowflake data is encrypted at rest regardless of schema type. Managed Access is about grant control, not encryption.

d.text: Managed Access schemas prevent SELECT queries from non-owner roles
d.feedback: Roles can still query tables if they've been granted access by the schema owner. The restriction is on who can issue GRANTs, not on who can query.

q2.prompt: You're doing a quarterly access review. A role has SELECT on a table but hasn't queried it in 90+ days. What should you do?

a.text: Cross-reference with the team, notify them of the planned revocation, then REVOKE if they confirm it's unneeded
a.feedback: Correct! Best practice is: check query history, notify the affected team ("we're revoking in 7 days unless you confirm need"), then revoke. Revoking without warning can break things.

b.text: REVOKE immediately — unused grants are always wrong
b.feedback: Careful! Some access is precautionary (disaster recovery, quarterly reports). Always assess impact and notify before revoking in production.

c.text: Leave it alone — better to over-grant than risk breaking something
c.feedback: This is how privilege drift happens. Every unnecessary grant increases attack surface. The right approach is to verify need and revoke if truly stale.

d.text: Delete the role entirely since it's clearly inactive
d.feedback: The role may be actively used for other objects — just not this particular table. Dropping a role is far more destructive than revoking a single grant.

q3.prompt: Which command shows you all roles that have privileges on a specific table?

a.feedback: Correct! SHOW GRANTS ON an object lists every privilege granted on that object and which role holds it. This is your "who can access this?" tool.

b.feedback: That shows what privileges a specific role has — the reverse question. You want SHOW GRANTS ON TABLE to see all roles with access to a specific object.

c.feedback: That shows which users/parent roles hold a specific role. You want SHOW GRANTS ON TABLE to see who has access to the object.

d.feedback: DESCRIBE shows the table's column definitions, not its access grants. Use SHOW GRANTS ON TABLE for privilege information.

q4.prompt: Why is REVOKE considered more dangerous than GRANT in production?

a.text: Because REVOKE takes effect immediately and can break downstream queries, dashboards, and pipelines the moment it's executed
a.feedback: Correct! GRANT is additive (nothing breaks), but REVOKE is subtractive — it can instantly break running workloads. Always check dependencies and coordinate before revoking in production.

b.text: Because REVOKE is irreversible — you can never re-grant the same privilege
b.feedback: REVOKE is reversible — you can always GRANT the same privilege again. The danger is the immediate breakage during the window between revoke and re-grant.

c.text: Because REVOKE requires ACCOUNTADMIN while GRANT does not
c.feedback: Both GRANT and REVOKE can be issued by object owners or roles with MANAGE GRANTS. The privilege requirements are similar. The danger is operational, not privilege-based.

d.text: Because REVOKE deletes the underlying data from the table
d.feedback: REVOKE only removes the privilege — it never touches the data itself. The danger is that consumers instantly lose access to data they may depend on.
